tool.name: Express
tool.tagline: Minimal, unopinionated web framework for Node.js
tool.description: Express is the most widely used web framework for Node.js: a thin layer over the http module that adds routing, a middleware pipeline and convenient request and response helpers. It is used to build JSON APIs, server-rendered sites and backend services, and its middleware model shaped most of the Node web ecosystem. Express 5 adds native async error handling and a safer routing syntax.

glossary.def: A small, widely used web framework for Node.js. It decides which of your functions answers each HTTP request and adds helpers for reading requests and sending responses.
In Express, a rule pairing an HTTP method and a URL path with the function to run for matching requests, such as GET /users/:id.
A named part of a route path, written with a colon like :id. The text in that place of the URL ends up in req.params, as a string.
Middleware that reads the data sent with a request, such as JSON or a submitted form, and puts the result on req.body.
A package that fills an HTML template with data to build a page on the server; Express calls it through res.render.
In Express, a mini-app made with express.Router() that holds its own routes and middleware and is attached to the app under a path prefix.
The path prefix under which middleware or a router is attached with app.use, such as /api. Inside, paths are seen without that prefix.
An Express middleware with four parameters (err, req, res, next). Express calls it only when something earlier failed, so it can send the error response.
A file or folder whose name starts with a dot, such as .env or .git, usually holding private settings. Express 5 refuses to serve them by default.
On the web, the scheme, host name and port at the start of a URL, such as https://app.example.com. Two URLs with any of these different are different origins.
The browser rule that a page's JavaScript may only read responses from its own origin, unless the other server allows it with CORS headers.
An OPTIONS request a browser sends before certain cross-origin requests, asking the server which methods and headers it allows.
A longer-lived token used only to get a new short-lived access token when the old one expires, so users don't have to log in again.
A testing package that sends real HTTP requests to an Express app in the same process, without you starting a server, and lets you check the responses.
An Express middleware package that adds a set of security-related response headers, such as Content-Security-Policy, with sensible defaults.
A response header listing where a page may load scripts, styles and other resources from, so a script injected by an attacker is refused.
A popular JavaScript and TypeScript library for describing what valid data looks like (a schema) and checking and converting data against it.
A bug where code copies every field a client sent into a database record, so an attacker can set fields they shouldn't, such as role: admin.
A standard file format that describes an HTTP API — every route, its inputs and its responses — from which docs and client code can be generated.
A response header holding a short label for one version of a response. The browser sends it back; if nothing changed, the server can answer 304 with no body.
A cache with a size limit that drops the least recently used entry when it is full, so the most-used results stay.
A slow pattern where code runs one database query to get a list, then one more query for each item in it, instead of fetching everything in one or two queries.
The Express team's middleware for reading file uploads sent as multipart/form-data; it puts files on req.file or req.files.
The request body format browsers use to upload files from a form: the body is split into parts, one per form field or file.
A time-limited address for uploading or downloading one file directly at a cloud storage service, signed by your server so no password is needed.
The first few bytes of a file, which identify its real type (for example, every PNG starts with the same 8 bytes), whatever its name says.
A unique id given to each incoming request and included in every log line about it, so all records for one request can be found together.
Writing each log entry as data with named fields (usually one JSON object per line) instead of a free-text sentence, so tools can filter and count them.
An open standard and set of libraries for collecting traces, metrics and logs from programs and sending them to any monitoring tool.
In tracing, a timed record of one step of handling a request, such as a database query. The spans of one request together show where its time went.
Handling the HTTPS encryption at a proxy or load balancer, which then forwards plain HTTP to the app behind it.
Express's internal record for one app.use or route registration: a compiled path matcher plus the function to call when it matches.
The number of parameters a function declares, available in JavaScript as fn.length. Express uses it to tell error handlers (4) from normal middleware.
A function that takes options and returns a new, configured function or object, such as express.json(options) returning a middleware.
A TypeScript declaration that adds properties to types defined in another package, such as a user field on Express's Request type.
A script that rewrites source code automatically, for example to move a project to a new version of a library.

concepts.name: What Express is
concepts.summary: Express is a small web framework on top of Node's http module that adds routes, middleware and request/response helpers.
concepts.why: It is the most widely used Node web framework, and most Node server code you'll read is built on it or on its ideas.
concepts.body:
When a browser opens a page, or an app loads data, it is the **client**: it sends an HTTP request to a server, and the server sends back a response. Node.js can be that server by itself. Its built-in `node:http` module hands your code each request and lets you write the response. But it hands it over raw: you look at the URL yourself, decide which code should answer, and read and write headers by hand.

**Express** is a small package that does that plumbing for you. It is a **web framework**: a library that gives a server its shape. You write the pieces that answer requests, and Express decides which piece to call for each one. On top of Node's http module it adds three things:

- **Routing**: you list **routes**, rules such as "when a GET request for `/users/42` arrives, run this function". **GET** is the HTTP method a browser uses to fetch a page; **POST** is the usual one for sending data, such as a filled-in form.
- **Middleware**: functions every request passes through on its way to your route, like stations on an assembly line. Each does one job — reading the data the request carries, checking who is logged in — then hands the request on.
- **Helpers on `req` and `res`**, the objects that stand for the request and the response: `req.params`, `req.query`, `res.json()`, `res.status()`, `res.redirect()` and more.

What Express deliberately leaves out: talking to a database, checking that incoming data makes sense, signing users in, how to arrange your project's files, and how to fill HTML pages with data. You add those from other packages, so your choices — not the framework's — shape the app.

This course targets **Express 5**, released in 2024 and the default on npm since 5.1 (March 2025). Compared with Express 4, errors in `async` route functions now reach the code that deals with errors automatically, the rules for writing route paths are stricter and safer, and long-outdated features are gone. It needs Node 18 or newer.

Where Express fits: JSON **APIs** — servers that other programs call to get or change data, rather than pages for people — as well as websites whose pages are built on the server, and small internal services. Fastify, Koa and NestJS solve similar problems; routes, middleware and request/response objects carry straight over.

Install it into a project with `npm install express`.
concepts.code:
# A new Express 5 project
mkdir my-api && cd my-api
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express          # installs Express 5 (latest)
npm ls express               # my-api@1.0.0 -> express@5.x
takeaways: Express = routes + middleware + req/res helpers on top of node:http
It is minimal: you choose the database, the data checks and the project layout
Express 5 forwards async errors automatically and needs Node 18+
pitfalls: Following Express 4 tutorials word for word — some features and path rules changed in 5.

quiz.q: Which of these does Express provide out of the box?
options: A built-in way to store data in a database
Checks that incoming data is valid
quiz.explain: Express is minimal: routing, middleware and req/res helpers; databases, logins and data checks come from other packages.

concepts.name: Your first Express app
concepts.summary: Create an app, add a route, start listening on a port, and understand what each line does.
concepts.why: Every Express app, however large, starts from these same few lines.
concepts.body:
An Express app is created by calling `express()`. The result, usually named `app`, is two things at once: the object you configure, and the **request handler** — the function Node calls with each incoming request.

- `app.get(path, handler)` adds a route: when a GET request for `path` arrives, Express calls `handler(req, res)`.
- `res.send(body)` sends the response. It sets the `Content-Type` header from the body (HTML for strings, JSON for objects) and the `Content-Length`, then finishes the response.
- `app.listen(port, callback)` starts a **web server**: a program that waits for requests and answers them. It returns the server object, which you keep so you can stop it later.

A computer can run many servers at once, so each listens on its own **port**: a numbered door, such as 3000. The address `http://localhost:3000` means "port 3000 on this computer" — **localhost** is the name every computer uses for itself.

Read the port from an environment variable (`process.env.PORT`) so hosting services can choose it. In Express 5, if the server can't start — say another program already uses that port (`EADDRINUSE`) — the error is passed to the `listen` callback, so check its first argument.

Run the app with `node --watch server.js` while developing; it restarts on every save. Then open `http://localhost:3000` in your browser.

Two habits worth forming from day one:

- **Keep the app separate from the server.** Export `app` from `app.js` and call `listen` in `server.js`. Tests can then use the app without starting a server.
- **Every request must get a response.** If a handler neither responds nor passes the request on, the client keeps waiting until it gives up, after a fixed wait called a **timeout**.

When no route matches, Express answers with a default **404** ("not found") page: "Cannot GET /nope". You'll replace it with your own later.
takeaways: `express()` creates the app; `app.get` adds a route; `app.listen` starts a server
Keep `app` (exported) separate from `listen` so tests can use it
Every request must end with a response
pitfalls: Hard-coding the port instead of reading `process.env.PORT`.

quiz.q: A GET request arrives for a path with no matching route and no custom handler. What does the client get?
options: The response of the first registered route
quiz.explain: Express's final handler answers unmatched requests with 404 "Cannot GET /path".

concepts.name: Routing: methods and paths
concepts.summary: Map HTTP methods and URL paths to handlers with app.get/post/put/delete, app.all and app.route.
concepts.why: Routes are what your server offers to the outside world; organising them well keeps an app understandable.
concepts.body:
A route is **method + path + one or more handlers**. Express has a function for each HTTP method: `app.get`, `app.post`, `app.put`, `app.patch`, `app.delete`, plus `app.all` for every method. By convention GET reads, POST creates, PUT and PATCH change, and DELETE removes.

Routes are checked **in the order you register them**, and the first one that matches and sends a response wins. Put specific routes before general ones: `/users/me` must come before `/users/:id`, or `me` is treated as an id.

Path matching details:

- Matching is case-insensitive and ignores a trailing slash by default (`/about` matches `/about/`).
- The query string is not part of the path: `/search?q=x` matches `/search`.
- `HEAD` requests are answered by your `GET` routes automatically, without a body.
- You can pass an array of paths: `app.get(["/", "/home"], handler)`.

When several methods share a path, `app.route(path)` chains them and avoids repeating the string:

```javascript
app.route("/books")
  .get(listBooks)
  .post(createBook);
```

A route can take **several handlers**; each calls `next()` to pass control to the following one. That is how middleware for just one route (checking a login, loading a record) is attached: `app.delete("/posts/:id", requireLogin, deletePost)`.

Express 5 dropped `app.del()` — use `app.delete()`. If a path exists but not for the requested method, Express returns 404, not 405; add an `app.all` fallback for that path if you want a proper `405 Method Not Allowed` with an `Allow` header.
takeaways: Routes match in registration order — specific before general
`app.route(path)` chains several methods on one path
A route can have several handlers linked with `next()`
pitfalls: Declaring `/users/:id` before `/users/me`, so `me` is captured as an id.

quiz.q: Routes are registered as GET /items/:id then GET /items/new. What handles GET /items/new?
quiz.explain: Express tries routes in order, and /items/:id matches first with id = 'new'.

concepts.name: Route parameters, wildcards and query strings
concepts.summary: Read values from the URL with :params, make parts optional with braces, match the rest of a path with *name, and read `req.query`.
concepts.why: Almost every route reads an id from the path or filters from the query string.
concepts.body:
**Route parameters** are named parts of a path that start with a colon. Whatever the URL has in that place appears on `req.params`, always as a **string**:

```javascript
app.get("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", (req, res) => {
  const { userId, postId } = req.params;   // "42", "7"
});
```

Convert and check them yourself: `Number(req.params.userId)` may be `NaN`. Special characters written in URL form, like `%20` for a space, are turned back into normal text for you.

Express 5 has new rules for writing paths (from the path-to-regexp library, version 8), stricter than Express 4's:

- **Optional parts** use braces: `/files/:name{.:ext}` matches `/files/report` and `/files/report.pdf`. The old `?` suffix is gone.
- **Wildcards must be named.** A **wildcard** matches any number of path pieces: `/assets/*filepath` matches everything after `/assets/`, and `req.params.filepath` is an **array of pieces** (`["css", "site.css"]`). Use `/{*splat}` to also match `/` itself.
- Special characters such as `(`, `[`, `+` and `?` inside path strings are no longer allowed. Use an array of paths instead, or a **regular expression**: a JavaScript rule for matching text, such as `/^\/post\/\d+$/`.
- An optional parameter that isn't in the URL is simply missing from `req.params`.

The **query string** (`?page=2&tag=node`) is parsed into `req.query`. Express 5's default parser gives strings, or arrays of strings when a key repeats (`?tag=a&tag=b`). Nested names like `filter[age]=3` are not expanded unless you opt in with `app.set("query parser", "extended")`.

Treat `req.query` as **untrusted input**: data from outside that may be missing, wrong or deliberately harmful. In Express 5 you can't reassign it; every value might be missing, a string, or an array; and numbers need converting. Path parameters say *which* thing; query parameters filter and sort it, or split a long list into pages (**pagination**).
takeaways: `req.params` values are strings — convert and check them
Express 5: optional parts use `{}`; wildcards are named (`*name`) and give arrays
`req.query` is read-only, and each value may be absent, a string or an array
pitfalls: Using Express 4 paths like `/:id?` or `/*`, which throw at startup in Express 5.
Assuming `req.query.tag` is a string when a repeated key makes it an array.

quiz.q: In Express 5, which path matches both /docs and /docs/guide/intro?
quiz.explain: Braces make the named wildcard optional; the other forms are Express 4 syntax that Express 5 rejects.

quiz.q: A request to /users/abc hits app.get('/users/:id'). What is req.params.id?
quiz.explain: Parameters are plain strings; Express does no type conversion or checking.

concepts.name: The request object
concepts.summary: Read headers, cookies, the content type, and details about the caller and the connection from Express's req object.
concepts.why: Handlers decide what to do based on the request; knowing where each piece lives avoids reparsing by hand.
concepts.body:
`req` is Node's request object (an `IncomingMessage`) with Express additions. Besides `req.params`, `req.query` and `req.body` (next lessons), these are the members you'll use most:

- `req.method`, `req.path` (the path without the query string), `req.originalUrl` (the full URL as received), `req.baseUrl` (the prefix a group of routes is attached under; a later lesson covers it).
- `req.get(name)` — read a header; upper or lower case doesn't matter: `req.get("Content-Type")`, `req.get("Authorization")`.
- `req.accepts(types)` — the client's `Accept` header lists the formats it can handle; this picks the one it prefers from those you offer.
- `req.cookies` — only if the `cookie-parser` middleware is installed; Express doesn't read cookies by itself.
- `req.app` — the app itself, handy in files that don't import it.

`req.is(type)` checks what kind of data was sent with the request. The request's `Content-Type` header names a **MIME type**: a standard label for a kind of content, such as `application/json` or `text/html`. `req.is("application/json")` returns the matching type or `false`.

Some members describe the caller and the connection. `req.ip` is the client's **IP address**, the number that identifies a computer on the network. `req.protocol` is `http` or `https`, `req.secure` is true for https, and `req.hostname` is the site name the request was sent to.

In production, requests often pass through another server first, which forwards them to yours: a **proxy**. Then `req.ip` and `req.protocol` describe the proxy, not the real client, until you configure the `trust proxy` setting (an Advanced lesson).

Everything on `req` that comes from the client is **untrusted**: headers can be faked, and body data can have any shape. Check it before you rely on it.

Middleware often **attaches data to `req`** for later handlers, such as `req.user` once it has checked who is logged in. For other per-request values, Express also offers `res.locals`. Keep such additions few and documented; in TypeScript, declare their types.

`req` is also a readable stream, which matters when you process large uploads piece by piece instead of reading them whole.
takeaways: `req.get()` reads headers; `req.is()` checks the content type; `req.accepts()` picks a format
`req.originalUrl` keeps the full URL; `req.path` leaves out the query string
`req.ip` and `req.protocol` need `trust proxy` behind a proxy
Treat all request data as untrusted
pitfalls: Expecting `req.cookies` to exist without installing cookie-parser.

quiz.q: A request for /api/users?x=1 arrives at a route for /api/users. What is req.originalUrl?
quiz.explain: originalUrl keeps the full URL as received, query string included; req.path would be /api/users.

concepts.name: Sending responses
concepts.summary: Send JSON, text, files, redirects and status codes with res.json, res.send, res.status, res.sendFile and friends.
concepts.why: Correct status codes, headers and bodies are what the programs calling your server actually rely on.
concepts.body:
Every request ends with exactly one response. Express's `res` helpers make the common cases one line:

- `res.json(value)` — turn a value into JSON and send it with `Content-Type: application/json`. The usual choice for APIs.
- `res.send(body)` — strings are sent as HTML, Buffers byte for byte, objects as JSON.
- `res.status(code)` — set the status; it returns `res`, so chain it: `res.status(201).json(item)`. In Express 5 it throws on invalid codes (non-integers, or outside 100–999).
- `res.sendStatus(code)` — status plus its standard text as body; `res.status(204).end()` for an empty response.
- `res.set(name, value)` / `res.get(name)` — set or read a header of the response; `res.type("csv")` sets the `Content-Type` header from a file extension.
- `res.redirect([status,] url)` — tell the client to load another URL instead (an **HTTP redirect**). 302 by default; use 301/308 for permanent moves. Express 5 removed the magic `"back"` value; use `req.get("Referrer") || "/"`.
- `res.sendFile(absolutePath)` and `res.download(path, filename)` — stream a file with the right headers; use the `root` option when the file name comes from the user.
- `res.cookie(name, value, options)` / `res.clearCookie(name)`.
- `res.render(view, data)` — build an HTML page from a **template**, an HTML file with blanks that are filled in from `data`. It needs a **view engine**: a package that does the filling, set up with `app.set("view engine", ...)`.

Common mistakes:

- **Responding twice.** Calling `res.json` and then falling through to another `res.send` throws "Cannot set headers after they are sent". Use `return res.json(...)` to stop the handler.
- **Wrong status codes.** `200` for success with a body, `201` for created, `204` for success without a body, `400` for invalid input, `401` not logged in, `403` logged in but not allowed, `404` not found, `409` conflict, `500` for your bugs.
- Express 5 removed the old two-argument forms such as `res.json(obj, 201)` and `res.send(200)`; always use `res.status()`.
takeaways: Chain `res.status(code).json(data)`; use `return` to stop the handler
Send exactly one response per request
Use precise status codes: 201 created, 204 no content, 4xx client errors
Express 5: `res.redirect(status, url)`; no `"back"`, no `res.json(obj, status)`
pitfalls: Forgetting `return` after an early response, then sending a second one.

quiz.q: A handler calls res.status(404).json({...}) inside an if, without return, and later res.json(item). What happens when the if runs?
options: Only the 404 is sent; the second call is ignored silently
The client gets both bodies concatenated
An error is thrown: headers already sent
quiz.explain: The second send tries to set headers on a finished response and throws ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT.

concepts.name: Parsing JSON and form bodies
concepts.summary: Read the data a client sends with express.json() and express.urlencoded(), set size limits, and handle malformed input.
concepts.why: Routes that receive data — usually POST, PUT and PATCH — are useless until you can read what the client sent.
concepts.body:
A request can carry data after its headers: the **request body**, such as the JSON an app sends or the answers in a submitted form. Express doesn't read it by default; it is still a raw stream. Add the built-in **body parsers**, middleware that reads the body and turns it into a JavaScript value:

- `app.use(express.json())` — for `Content-Type: application/json`. The result appears on `req.body`.
- `app.use(express.urlencoded())` — for classic HTML form submissions (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`).
- `express.text()` and `express.raw()` — for text, and for the bytes exactly as they arrived. `raw` gives a Buffer, which you need when a service signs the exact bytes it sends you and you must check that signature.

Each parser only acts when the request's `Content-Type` matches its `type` option. In Express 5, if no parser ran, **`req.body` is `undefined`** (Express 4 gave `{}`), so code like `req.body.name` throws when a request arrives without a JSON content type. Write `req.body?.name`, or check the body first.

Options worth knowing:

- `limit` — maximum body size, default `"100kb"`. Larger bodies get a **413** error. Raise it only where needed, ideally on one route: `app.post("/import", express.json({ limit: "5mb" }), handler)`.
- `strict` (json, default `true`) — only accept objects and arrays at the top level.
- `extended` (urlencoded) — Express 5 defaults to `false`, a simple parser; set `true` to expand nested names like `a[b]=c` with the `qs` library.

Malformed JSON produces an error with `status` 400 and `type: "entity.parse.failed"`. It goes to your error-handling middleware (a later lesson; the code below shows a small one). Answer with a helpful 400 there, not a **stack trace** — the list of function calls that led to the error, which reveals how your code works inside.

`req.body` is untrusted: it can be any JSON shape, including a plain number, unexpected properties, or `__proto__` keys. Check it carefully (a later lesson) before using it. File uploads (`multipart/form-data`) need a different parser, such as multer.
takeaways: Add `express.json()` / `express.urlencoded()`; nothing is parsed by default
Express 5: `req.body` is `undefined` when no parser ran
Default limit is 100kb; raise it per route when needed
Malformed JSON becomes a 400-status error for your error-handling middleware
pitfalls: Testing with curl but forgetting `-H 'Content-Type: application/json'`, so `req.body` is undefined.

quiz.q: A client POSTs valid JSON with Content-Type: text/plain to an app using express.json(). What is req.body in Express 5?
quiz.explain: express.json() only parses matching content types; with no parser run, Express 5 leaves req.body undefined.

concepts.name: Serving static files
concepts.summary: Serve images, CSS, JavaScript and HTML files from a folder with express.static, with URL prefixes, caching and safe defaults.
concepts.why: The files a website's pages load in the browser — styles, scripts, images — are served this way in many apps.
concepts.body:
Many files never change while the server runs: images, CSS, the JavaScript a browser runs, ready-made HTML pages. These are **static files**: the server sends them as they are instead of computing a response. `express.static(root, options)` is built-in middleware that serves them from a folder. A request for `/css/site.css` is answered with `root/css/site.css` if that file exists; otherwise it calls `next()` and later routes get a chance.

```javascript
app.use(express.static(path.join(import.meta.dirname, "public")));
```

Always pass an **absolute path** built from `import.meta.dirname`; a relative path depends on the folder the program was started from.

Useful options:

- **Mount path**: `app.use("/static", express.static(dir))` serves `dir/logo.png` at `/static/logo.png`. The prefix it is mounted under is removed before the file is looked up.
- **Several folders**: call `express.static` more than once; they are tried in order.
- **index** files: a request for a folder serves its `index.html`; turn that off with `index: false`.

Browsers keep copies of files they have downloaded. `maxAge: "1d"` sets the `Cache-Control` header, saying a copy stays good for a day. Tools that package browser code often put a fingerprint of the contents in each file name (`app.3f9a1c.js`), so a changed file always gets a new name; for those, use `maxAge: "1y", immutable: true`. The `ETag` and `Last-Modified` headers are on by default, so browsers can cheaply ask "has this changed?".

Some websites are a single HTML page whose JavaScript draws every screen in the browser: a **single-page application**. Its URLs, like `/settings`, aren't real files, so after the static middleware add a catch-all route that returns `index.html`: `app.get("/{*splat}", (req, res) => res.sendFile(indexPath))`. Put your API routes before it.

Safe defaults: a request like `/../secret` that tries to climb out of the folder (**path traversal**) is blocked. In Express 5, files and folders whose names start with a dot (**dotfiles**, often private settings such as `.env`) are ignored with a 404. If you need the standard `/.well-known` folder, which some services check to confirm you own a site, serve it explicitly with `{ dotfiles: "allow" }`.

In production, a **CDN** — a network of servers around the world that keeps copies of your files close to users — or a dedicated web server such as nginx in front of Node often serves these files faster and keeps the load off Node. `express.static` remains perfect for development and smaller apps.
takeaways: `express.static(absDir)` serves files and calls `next()` when none matches
Use a mount path; give fingerprinted file names a long `maxAge` and `immutable`
Express 5 ignores dotfiles by default; allow `.well-known` explicitly
pitfalls: Passing a relative directory, which breaks when the app is started from another folder.

quiz.q: app.use('/static', express.static('/srv/app/public')). Which URL serves /srv/app/public/img/a.png?
quiz.explain: The mount path prefix replaces the directory root: /static + /img/a.png.

concepts.name: Middleware and next()
concepts.summary: Understand middleware functions (req, res, next), how app.use mounts them, and why order matters.
concepts.why: Middleware is Express's core idea: request logs, body parsing, login checks, CORS and error handling are all middleware.
concepts.body:
A **middleware** is a function `(req, res, next)` that runs during a request. It can do any of three things:

- **Respond** and end the cycle (`res.status(401).json(...)`).
- **Modify** `req`/`res` and call `next()` to pass control to the next middleware or route.
- **Fail** by calling `next(err)` (or, in Express 5, throwing or rejecting), which skips straight to **error-handling middleware**, the special functions that deal with failures (a later lesson).

If it does none of these, the request hangs.

`app.use(fn)` runs `fn` for every request; `app.use("/admin", fn)` only for paths starting with `/admin` (a prefix match: `/admin`, `/admin/users`, not `/administrator`). Inside, `req.url` is relative to the mount path while `req.originalUrl` keeps the full URL. Route handlers are middleware too — `app.get(path, a, b, c)` is a chain of three.

**Order is everything.** Express runs matching middleware and routes in exactly the order you registered them. Typical order:

- Request-wide setup: request ID, logging, security headers, CORS, body parsers.
- Checking who is logged in (setting `req.user`).
- Routes and routers.
- A 404 handler for anything unmatched.
- Error handlers (four arguments) last.

A logger registered after your routes never sees requests that routes answered; a body parser registered after a route leaves `req.body` undefined in that route.

To run code **after** the response is sent — timing, metrics, logs — don't wait in the middleware; listen for `res.on("finish")`. Because `async` middleware is supported in Express 5, you can `await` inside and simply call `next()` when done; a rejection is forwarded as an error.

Use `res.locals` to pass per-request data to later middleware and templates without polluting `req`.
takeaways: Middleware either responds, calls `next()`, or passes an error
`app.use(path, fn)` is a prefix match; registration order is execution order
Use `res.on('finish')` for after-response work and `res.locals` for per-request data
pitfalls: Registering body parsers or auth after the routes that need them.
Forgetting to call `next()` in a non-responding middleware, hanging the request.

quiz.q: A middleware logs and doesn't call next() or send a response. What does the client experience?
options: The request hangs until it times out
quiz.explain: Without next() or a response, Express has nothing more to do and the response is never finished.

quiz.q: app.use('/api', fn) is registered. For which request does fn run?
quiz.explain: app.use mounts by path prefix on segment boundaries, so /api and anything under /api/ match.

concepts.name: Routers and project structure
concepts.summary: Split an app into express.Router files, mount them under prefixes, and organise files by feature.
concepts.why: Single-file apps become unmaintainable fast; routers are how Express apps stay modular.
concepts.body:
`express.Router()` creates a **router**, a mini-application: it has `get`, `post`, `use`, `route` and `param` like `app`, but no server of its own. You **mount** it under a prefix with `app.use("/users", usersRouter)`, and inside the router paths are relative: `router.get("/:id")` answers `/users/:id`.

Routers give you:

- **Modularity** — one file per resource or feature, each exporting a router.
- **Middleware for one group** — `router.use(requireLogin)` only affects that router's routes.
- **Versioning** — mount the same or different routers under `/v1` and `/v2`.

By default a child router does **not** see parameters from its mount path. For nested resources like `/projects/:projectId/tasks`, create the child with `express.Router({ mergeParams: true })` so `req.params.projectId` is visible.

A structure that scales well for APIs groups by feature, not by technical layer:

```
src/
  app.js            creates app, global middleware, mounts routers
  server.js         listen + shutdown
  config.js
  users/
    users.router.js
    users.service.js    business logic, no req/res
    users.schema.js     validation
  middleware/
```

Keep **handlers thin**: parse and validate input, call a service function, map the result to a response. Business logic in plain functions is easy to test on its own, with small **unit tests**, and to reuse from scripts.

`router.param("id", fn)` runs `fn` once per request whenever a route with `:id` matches — a neat way to load a record and 404 early. Express 5 also re-exposes `app.router`, the app's own base router.
takeaways: `express.Router()` is a mountable mini-app with relative paths
Use `mergeParams: true` for nested resources
Organise by feature; keep handlers thin and logic in services
pitfalls: Forgetting `mergeParams` and finding the parent's `req.params` empty in a nested router.

quiz.q: A router mounted at /teams/:teamId/members needs teamId. What must you do?
options: Create it with express.Router({ mergeParams: true })
quiz.explain: Child routers only receive the parent's params when created with mergeParams: true.

concepts.name: Error handling and async errors
concepts.summary: Write 404 handlers and error-handling middleware, rely on Express 5 passing on failed async calls, and map errors to status codes.
concepts.why: Consistent error responses — and no leaked stack traces — are the difference between a robust API and a fragile one.
concepts.body:
An **error-handling middleware** has four parameters: `(err, req, res, next)`. Express recognises it by that number of parameters, so you must declare all four even if you don't use `next`. Register error handlers **after** all routes.

How errors reach it:

- Synchronous code: a `throw` in a handler or middleware is caught by Express.
- Callbacks: call `next(err)` explicitly.
- **Async code (Express 5):** if a handler or middleware returns a promise that **rejects** — an `async` function that throws or awaits a failing call — Express calls `next(err)` for you. Express 4 needed wrappers like `express-async-errors` for this; Express 5 doesn't.

One catch: errors thrown in a *callback* inside an async function (say, inside a `setTimeout` or an event listener) are not part of the returned promise, so Express can't see them. Promisify such code.

Once an error is passed, Express **skips all regular middleware** and runs only error handlers. A handler can respond, or call `next(err)` to delegate to the next one. If you never handle it, Express's default handler responds 500 and prints the stack trace — including in the response body when `NODE_ENV` is not `production`.

A good approach:

- Throw your own error classes with a `status` (or `statusCode`) and a safe message: `throw new HttpError(404, "Project not found")`.
- Add a **404 handler** after the routes: `app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json(...))` — unmatched requests aren't errors, they just fall through.
- In the final error handler, log the full error, respond with the status if it's a client error, and a generic message for 500s. Never send stack traces to clients.
- If `res.headersSent` is true (the error happened mid-stream), delegate to `next(err)` so Express closes the connection.
takeaways: Error handlers take exactly four arguments and go after all routes
Express 5 forwards rejected promises from async handlers automatically
A 404 handler is ordinary middleware at the end, not an error handler
Log details server-side; send safe messages to clients
pitfalls: Declaring an error handler with three parameters, so Express treats it as normal middleware.
Throwing inside a setTimeout or event callback in an async handler, which Express can't catch.

quiz.q: In Express 5, an async route handler awaits a database call that rejects. What happens?
options: The process crashes with an unhandled rejection
Express passes the error to the error-handling middleware
quiz.explain: Express 5 attaches to the returned promise and calls next(err) when it rejects.

quiz.q: Why is app.use((req, res) => res.status(404)...) placed after all routes?
options: It should only run when no earlier route or middleware responded
Express requires 404 handlers to be last syntactically
quiz.explain: Middleware runs in order; a catch-all at the end only sees requests nothing else handled.

concepts.name: Validating input
concepts.summary: Validate and coerce params, query and body with a schema library such as Zod, and return clear 400 errors.
concepts.why: Unvalidated input causes crashes, data corruption and security holes; validation at the edge prevents all three.
concepts.body:
Everything in `req.params`, `req.query` and `req.body` is untrusted and loosely typed. **Validation** means checking that data has the right shape and values before you use it. Do it **at the boundary**, in the route, before the data reaches business logic. Hand-written `if` checks don't scale; use a **schema library**, where you describe what valid data looks like (the **schema**) and the library checks it. Zod is popular in the TypeScript world; Joi, Yup, Valibot, AJV (which uses the JSON Schema standard) and express-validator are common alternatives.

A schema does three jobs at once:

- **Validates** shape and constraints (types, lengths, ranges, formats).
- **Coerces/transforms** — query strings are strings, so `z.coerce.number()` turns `"20"` into `20`; defaults fill missing fields.
- **Strips unknown keys** — Zod's `z.object` drops fields you didn't declare, preventing **mass assignment** bugs: a client sending an extra `"role": "admin"` that your code copies into the database.

Use `safeParse` and turn failures into a **400 Bad Request** with field-level messages so clients can fix their request. Never pass the raw `req.body` to your database layer; pass the parsed result.

A small reusable middleware keeps routes tidy: `validate({ body: schema })` parses and stores the result. In Express 5 `req.query` is a read-only getter, so don't try to overwrite it; store the parsed values elsewhere, such as `res.locals` or a property like `req.valid`.

What belongs where:

- **Schema validation** (shape, format) at the edge.
- **Business rules** (email already registered, insufficient balance) in services — usually 409 or 422.
- **Database constraints** as a last line of defence.

Also validate **path params** — an id that isn't a number (or whatever format your ids use) should be a 400 or 404, not a database error.
takeaways: Validate params, query and body at the route boundary with a schema
Schemas also coerce types and strip unknown fields
Return 400 with field-level details; pass only parsed data onward
Express 5's `req.query` is read-only — store parsed values elsewhere
pitfalls: Spreading `req.body` straight into a database update (mass assignment).

quiz.q: Why is z.coerce.number() typically used for query parameters rather than z.number()?
options: Query values arrive as strings and must be converted
quiz.explain: req.query values are strings; coerce converts "20" to 20 before validating.

concepts.name: Designing a REST API
concepts.summary: Model resources with nouns and HTTP methods, use correct status codes, paginate, and keep error formats consistent.
concepts.why: A predictable API is easier to consume, document and evolve without breaking clients.
concepts.body:
**REST** is a widely used set of conventions for designing HTTP APIs, so anyone calling yours can guess how it works. The core ideas:

**Resources are nouns, methods are verbs.** `/articles` is a collection, `/articles/42` one item. Use `GET` to read, `POST` to create, `PUT` to replace, `PATCH` to partially update, `DELETE` to remove. Avoid verbs in paths like `/getArticles` or `/deleteArticle`.

**Status codes carry meaning:**

- `200 OK` with a body; `201 Created` plus a `Location` header pointing to the new item; `204 No Content` for successful deletes.
- `400` invalid input, `401` not authenticated, `403` authenticated but not allowed, `404` not found, `409` conflict (duplicate), `422` well-formed but not acceptable, `429` too many requests.
- `500` only for your bugs; `503` when a dependency is down.

**Idempotency.** An operation is **idempotent** if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` must be, so clients can safely send them again after a failure (a **retry**); `POST` isn't. For payments and other critical creates, accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and return the stored result on retries.

**Collections** should paginate: `?limit=20&cursor=...`, where the cursor is a marker the previous response handed back for where the next page starts (this scales better than `?page=`), return the next cursor, and cap `limit`. Filtering and sorting go in the query string: `?status=open&sort=-createdAt`.

**One error shape** everywhere, e.g. `{ "error": { "code": "not_found", "message": "..." } }` or the RFC 9457 problem-details format. Clients can then handle errors generically.

**Evolve without breaking:** add fields freely, never rename or remove them silently. When you must break, version with a path prefix (`/v2`) or a header.

Document the API with **OpenAPI**, a standard file format that describes every route; docs and ready-made client libraries generated from it pay for themselves quickly.
takeaways: Nouns for resources, HTTP methods for actions
201 + Location on create, 204 on delete, precise 4xx codes
Paginate collections (prefer cursors) and cap page size
One consistent error format; evolve additively
pitfalls: Returning 200 with `{ success: false }` for errors, which defeats HTTP-level handling.

quiz.q: A client retries a DELETE /items/5 after a timeout; the item is already gone. Which design is most RESTful?
options: Treat DELETE as idempotent: return 204 (or 404) without side effects
quiz.explain: DELETE is idempotent: repeating it must not cause additional effects, so a 204 or 404 is appropriate.

concepts.name: CORS for browser clients
concepts.summary: Understand the same-origin policy and preflight requests, and configure the cors middleware with explicit origins.
concepts.why: Your API is unusable from a website on another origin until CORS is set up — and dangerous if set up carelessly.
concepts.body:
An **origin** is the scheme, host name and port at the start of a URL: `https://app.example.com` and `https://api.example.com` are different origins. Browsers enforce the **same-origin policy**: JavaScript on `https://app.example.com` may send a request to `https://api.example.com`, but cannot *read* the response unless the API says so with **CORS** headers. CORS is a browser rule; curl, servers and mobile apps ignore it. It doesn't prove who is calling — it only controls which websites' scripts may read your responses.

The mechanics:

- For **simple** requests (GET/POST with basic headers), the browser sends the request with an `Origin` header and checks the response's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
- For anything else — `PUT`/`DELETE`, `Content-Type: application/json`, an `Authorization` header — the browser first sends a **preflight request**, an `OPTIONS` request asking permission (`Access-Control-Request-Method`, `-Headers`). Your server must answer it with the allowed methods and headers.
- To send cookies ("credentials" in CORS terms), the browser code sets `credentials: "include"` and the server must return `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` with a **specific** origin — `*` is not allowed with credentials.

The `cors` package handles all of this:

- `cors({ origin: ["https://app.example.com"] })` — allow a fixed list (it echoes the matching origin and sets `Vary: Origin`).
- `origin` can also be a function for dynamic checks, e.g. one domain per customer.
- `credentials: true`, `methods`, `allowedHeaders`, `exposedHeaders` (to let JS read custom response headers), `maxAge` (cache the preflight).

Mount it **before** your routes so preflights get answered. Avoid reflecting any origin with credentials — that lets every website make authenticated requests on your users' behalf. If the website and the API share an origin (for example, one server forwards `/api` requests to Express), you don't need CORS at all.
takeaways: CORS lets chosen origins' scripts read your responses; it doesn't prove identity
Non-simple requests trigger an OPTIONS preflight you must answer
Credentials require a specific origin, never `*`
Mount `cors()` before routes; allow-list origins
pitfalls: Using `origin: true` (reflect any origin) together with `credentials: true`.

quiz.q: A React app on localhost:5173 sends fetch(api, { method: 'PUT', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } }). What does the browser send first?
quiz.explain: PUT with a JSON content type is not a simple request, so the browser preflights with OPTIONS.

concepts.name: Authentication: sessions and JWTs
concepts.summary: Compare cookie sessions with JWT bearer tokens, hash passwords properly, and protect routes with login-checking middleware.
concepts.why: Nearly every real app needs to know who is calling, and auth mistakes are among the most damaging bugs.
concepts.body:
**Authentication** answers "who is this?" on every request. Two mainstream approaches:

**Server-side sessions.** A **session** is what the server remembers about one logged-in visitor. After login, the server stores the session data (the user's id) in a store such as Redis (a fast database that keeps data in memory) and sends the client a cookie containing only a random session id (`express-session`). Each request's cookie looks up the session.

- Easy to revoke (delete the session), small cookies, works naturally for browser apps.
- Needs a shared store when you run several copies of the app. Never use the default in-memory store in production.

**JWT bearer tokens.** A **JWT** (JSON Web Token) is a small piece of JSON the server signs with a secret, so it can later prove nobody altered it. After login the server signs one (`jsonwebtoken`) with claims like `sub` (the user id) and `exp` (expiry time). The client sends it back with every request as an **access token**, `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, and the server checks the signature without looking anything up.

- **Stateless** — the server keeps nothing per user — and convenient for APIs used by mobile apps and other services.
- Hard to revoke before expiry, so keep access tokens short-lived (minutes) and pair them with **refresh tokens**, longer-lived tokens used only to get new access tokens. Pin the signing algorithm when verifying (`algorithms: ["HS256"]`).

For apps running in the browser, cookies are usually the safer way to carry the login: set them **`httpOnly`** (invisible to JavaScript, so XSS can't steal them), **`secure`** (sent only over HTTPS) and **`sameSite: "lax"`**. That last flag blocks most **CSRF** (cross-site request forgery): another website making your user's browser send requests to your app. Tokens stored in `localStorage` are readable by any injected script.

Always:

- Hash passwords with a slow algorithm — `bcrypt`, `argon2`, or Node's built-in `crypto.scrypt` — never plain SHA-256.
- Read secrets from environment variables.
- Return the same error for "unknown user" and "wrong password", and rate-limit login.

Protect routes with a middleware that checks the session or token, sets `req.user`, and responds 401 otherwise; check permissions (403) separately. For "Sign in with Google" and similar, use a library for OpenID Connect, the standard behind such logins, rather than writing your own.
takeaways: Sessions: server-side state + cookie id; easy revocation, needs a shared store
JWTs: signed, stateless, short-lived; pin the algorithm when verifying
Cookies for browsers: `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite`
Hash passwords with scrypt/bcrypt/argon2; 401 for unauthenticated, 403 for forbidden
pitfalls: Storing JWTs in localStorage in a browser app, exposing them to XSS.
Using express-session's default MemoryStore in production.

quiz.q: Why are JWT access tokens usually given short lifetimes?
options: Long tokens are too large for headers
They can't easily be revoked before they expire
quiz.explain: The server doesn't look them up, so a stolen token stays valid until exp; short lifetimes limit the damage.

quiz.q: Which cookie flag stops client-side JavaScript from reading the session cookie?
quiz.explain: httpOnly cookies are sent with requests but hidden from document.cookie.

concepts.name: Testing Express apps with supertest
concepts.summary: Test routes end to end in-process with supertest and node:test: status codes, bodies, headers and auth.
concepts.why: Tests that send real HTTP requests catch mistakes in routes, middleware order and response formats that tests of single functions (unit tests) miss.
concepts.body:
**supertest** sends real HTTP requests to your Express app without you starting a server: pass it the `app`, and it opens a temporary port for each request. This is why exporting `app` separately from `app.listen` matters.

```javascript
const res = await request(app).get("/users/1").set("Authorization", "Bearer t");
```

The returned response has `status`, `body` (parsed JSON), `headers` and `text`. You can assert with `node:assert` (or Jest/Vitest), or use supertest's chained `.expect(200)` / `.expect("Content-Type", /json/)`.

Useful techniques:

- **Sending data:** `.post("/users").send({ name: "Ada" })` sets the JSON content type automatically; `.query({ page: 2 })` builds the query string.
- **Cookies/sessions:** `request.agent(app)` keeps cookies between requests, so you can log in once and call protected routes.
- **Dependencies:** build the app with a function, `createApp({ db, mailer })`, so tests pass in fakes or a test database instead of patching modules. This is the single most useful design choice for testability.
- **Error paths:** test the 400, 401, 404 and 500 responses deliberately; they are where APIs most often regress. A test that hits a throwing route verifies that your error handler hides internal details.

What to test at which level:

- Services and plain functions: fast unit tests.
- Routes: supertest tests for each route's promised behaviour — status, body shape, headers.
- A handful of full end-to-end tests against a real database and server.

Run them with `node --test`. Keep tests independent: create fresh app state per test (`beforeEach`) instead of relying on order.
takeaways: `request(app)` tests over HTTP without starting a server yourself
Use an app factory to inject fake or test dependencies
`request.agent(app)` keeps cookies for session flows
Test error paths, not just the happy path
pitfalls: Importing a module that calls `app.listen()` at import time, leaving ports open and tests hanging.

quiz.q: Why does structuring code as createApp({ db }) help testing?
options: It makes the app start faster
Tests can pass a fake or test database without patching modules
quiz.explain: Passing collaborators in lets each test build an app with exactly the database or fakes it needs.

concepts.name: Security hardening: helmet and rate limiting
concepts.summary: Harden an Express app with helmet's security headers, rate limiting, body limits, safe cookies and up-to-date dependencies.
concepts.why: Default Express is minimal by design; production exposure needs explicit defences against common attacks.
concepts.body:
Express's own best-practice guide boils down to a short checklist. Work through it for every production app.

**Security headers with helmet.** The **helmet** package sets a sensible bundle of response headers that tell browsers to be stricter: `app.use(helmet())` adds `Content-Security-Policy` (limits where scripts and other resources load from — the strongest XSS mitigation for HTML apps), `Strict-Transport-Security` (forces HTTPS), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Cross-Origin-*` policies, and it removes `X-Powered-By`. Tune the CSP rules for the scripts your pages really load rather than disabling CSP. Pure JSON APIs need fewer headers but helmet's defaults are harmless there.

**Rate limiting.** A **rate limit** caps how many requests one client may make in a time window; `express-rate-limit` does it. Apply a generous global limit and strict ones on expensive or sensitive routes: login, password reset, signup, search. Its default memory store is per process; with several copies of the app, use a shared store (Redis). It counts per `req.ip`, so configure `trust proxy` correctly, or every user behind your **load balancer** (the server that spreads requests across your copies) shares one count.

**Limit input.** Keep body-parser `limit`s small, validate everything, cap pagination sizes, and set server timeouts so slow clients can't hold connections forever.

**Cookies.** `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite: "lax"` (or `"strict"`), a scoped `path`, and a non-default session cookie name so the technology you use is less obvious.

**CSRF.** If you authenticate with cookies, `sameSite` cookies stop most cross-site form posts; for older clients or `sameSite: "none"`, add CSRF tokens. Bearer tokens in headers aren't vulnerable to CSRF.

**Errors and info leaks.** Run with `NODE_ENV=production`, never return stack traces, and don't echo raw input into HTML without escaping.

**Dependencies.** `npm audit` in CI, keep Express and middleware updated, and watch the Express security-release announcements.
takeaways: `helmet()` adds CSP, HSTS, nosniff and more; tune CSP instead of disabling it
Rate-limit globally and strictly on auth routes; share the store across instances
Small body limits, server timeouts and validated input limit DoS
Secure cookie flags, NODE_ENV=production, patched dependencies
pitfalls: Rate limiting behind a proxy without `trust proxy`, so all users share the proxy's IP bucket.

quiz.q: Which header set by helmet is the main defence-in-depth against XSS in HTML responses?
quiz.explain: CSP restricts which scripts may run, so injected script tags are blocked even if escaping fails.

concepts.name: Performance and HTTP caching
concepts.summary: Speed up Express apps with production mode, compression, ETags, Cache-Control, application caching and keeping slow synchronous work out of handlers.
concepts.why: Most Express performance problems are fixed by caching and not doing work, rather than by micro-optimisation.
concepts.body:
Express itself is rarely the bottleneck; what your handlers do is. The big wins, roughly in order:

**Run in production mode.** `NODE_ENV=production` makes Express cache view templates and send less verbose errors, and many libraries take faster paths.

**Don't block the event loop.** Synchronous `fs`, `crypto` or giant `JSON.stringify` calls in a handler stall every request being handled at the same time. Use async APIs, stream large responses, and move heavy CPU work to worker threads.

**HTTP caching** lets browsers and CDNs skip requests entirely:

- `Cache-Control` tells caches how long a response is fresh: `public, max-age=300` for shared data, `private, no-cache` for per-user data that must be revalidated, `no-store` for sensitive data.
- **ETags**: an **ETag** is a short label for one version of a response. `res.send`/`res.json` add one by default. When the client sends `If-None-Match` with the same tag, Express replies `304 Not Modified` without a body. That saves data transfer, not server work — the handler still ran.
- `express.static` with long `maxAge` and `immutable` for fingerprinted assets.
- Set `Vary` when the response depends on a header (`Accept-Encoding`, `Origin`, `Authorization`).

**Application caching** saves the work itself: keep the results of expensive lookups in an in-process **LRU cache** (it drops the least recently used entries when full) with a **TTL** (time to live, after which an entry expires), or in Redis when several copies of the app must share it. Plan **cache invalidation** — how stale entries get removed when the data changes — before you add a cache.

**Compression.** The `compression` middleware shrinks responses with gzip; at scale, let nginx or the CDN do it and skip Node entirely for that work.

**Database access** usually dominates response time: add indexes, select only the columns you need, avoid **N+1 queries** (one query for a list, then one more per item), and use a connection pool.

Measure first: track per route the time within which 95% and 99% of requests finish (p95/p99), load-test with autocannon, and profile with `--cpu-prof` before changing code.
takeaways: Set NODE_ENV=production and keep sync work off the request path
Use Cache-Control, ETags and Vary to let clients and CDNs skip work
Cache expensive results with a TTL; plan invalidation
Measure p95/p99 and profile before optimising
pitfalls: Marking per-user responses `public`, letting a CDN serve one user's data to another.

quiz.q: A client sends If-None-Match with the current ETag of a JSON response. What does Express do by default?
options: Responds 304 Not Modified without a body after the handler runs
quiz.explain: Express compares the generated ETag with the request header and sends 304, but the handler still did its work.

concepts.name: Handling file uploads
concepts.summary: Accept file uploads with multer: size limits, file filtering, disk or memory storage, and sending files on to cloud storage.
concepts.why: Uploads are a common feature and a common way in for attackers; limits and checks are not optional.
concepts.body:
HTML forms and `FormData` send files as **multipart/form-data** — a body split into parts, one per form field or file — which `express.json()` and `express.urlencoded()` don't parse. **multer**, the Express team's upload middleware, does.

```javascript
const upload = multer({ dest: "uploads/", limits: { fileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024 } });
app.post("/avatar", upload.single("avatar"), handler);
```

- `upload.single(field)` puts one file on `req.file`; `upload.array(field, max)` and `upload.fields([...])` put several on `req.files`. Text fields land on `req.body`.
- Each file object has `originalname`, `mimetype`, `size`, and either `path` (disk storage) or `buffer` (memory storage).

Storage choices:

- **Disk** (`dest` or `multer.diskStorage`) — files are streamed to disk, so memory stays flat. Multer generates random filenames; never use `originalname` as a path.
- **Memory** (`multer.memoryStorage()`) — convenient for small files you process immediately (resize an avatar), dangerous for large ones because the whole file sits in RAM.
- For **object storage** (cloud file services such as Amazon S3), stream from disk after checking the file, or use a storage engine that streams directly. Many apps skip the server entirely: hand the client a **presigned URL** — a time-limited upload address signed by your server — and only store the resulting file name.

Always set **limits** — `fileSize`, `files`, `fields` — or a single request can fill your disk or memory. Exceeding them raises a `MulterError` with a code like `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE`, which you map to `413` in your error handler.

`mimetype` and the extension come from the client and can lie. Use `fileFilter` for a first check, then verify the content — check its **magic bytes** (the first bytes, which identify the real file type), or decode the image — before trusting it. Serve uploaded files from a separate domain or with `Content-Disposition: attachment` so a malicious HTML upload can't run in your origin.
takeaways: multer parses multipart/form-data; `req.file`/`req.files` plus `req.body`
Always set `limits`; map `MulterError` codes to 400/413
Disk storage for size, memory only for small files; never trust `originalname`
Client MIME types lie — verify content before use
pitfalls: Using memoryStorage without a fileSize limit, letting one upload exhaust RAM.
Saving files under the client-supplied original name, enabling overwrites and path tricks.

quiz.q: Why is multer's memoryStorage risky for a video-upload endpoint?
options: It loses the file's MIME type
The whole file is buffered in RAM, so large or concurrent uploads exhaust memory
quiz.explain: Memory storage keeps each file in a Buffer; big files multiply quickly across concurrent requests.

concepts.name: Logging and observability
concepts.summary: Add structured request logs with request IDs, log errors once with context, expose health-check routes, and trace requests with OpenTelemetry.
concepts.why: When production misbehaves, logs, metrics and traces are your only window into what happened.
concepts.body:
**Observability** means being able to answer "what is happening and why?" from the outside. For an Express service that's three signals.

**Structured logs.** Log JSON objects, not sentences, so your log platform can filter by field. **pino** with **pino-http** is fast and idiomatic; `morgan` is a simpler access logger. Each request should produce one access-log line with method, route, status, duration and a **request ID**, a unique id given to each request. Accept an incoming `X-Request-Id` (or generate one with `crypto.randomUUID()`), return it in the response, and include it in every log line so you can follow a request across services.

Rules of thumb:

- Log errors **once**, in the error handler, with the stack and request context — not at every layer that rethrows.
- Never log secrets, passwords, tokens or full request bodies; use redaction options.
- Use levels (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`) and set the level from the environment.
- Write to stdout and let the platform ship logs; don't manage log files in Node.

**Metrics.** Request rate, error rate and **latency** (how long requests take; p50/p95/p99 are the times within which half, 95% and 99% of them finish) per route, plus event-loop delay and memory. Expose them for Prometheus or push them via OpenTelemetry. Label them with the route's path template (`req.route?.path`, like `/users/:id`), not the raw URL, or every user id becomes a separate series to store.

**Traces.** **OpenTelemetry** is the open standard for this data. Its Node packages automatically measure Express, `http`, `fetch` and popular database client libraries, producing **spans** (timed records of each step) that show where a slow request spent its time across services.

**Health checks** are routes your platform calls to see if the app is fine: a cheap `/healthz` (liveness: the process is up) and a `/readyz` (readiness: dependencies reachable, not shutting down). Keep them out of access logs and rate limits.

Wrap context in `AsyncLocalStorage` so deep code can log with the request ID without passing it around.
takeaways: One structured access log per request, tagged with a request ID
Log errors once with context; redact secrets
Metrics by route path template; traces via OpenTelemetry
Separate liveness and readiness endpoints
pitfalls: Labelling metrics with the raw URL, creating an endless number of separate series.

quiz.q: Why include a request ID in responses and every log line?
options: It lets you correlate all logs (and other services' logs) for one request
quiz.explain: A shared ID ties together everything that happened while handling one request, across components.

concepts.name: Deploying behind a proxy
concepts.summary: Run Express behind a load balancer: the trust proxy setting, HTTPS, ports, process management and clean shutdowns.
concepts.why: Misconfigured proxies cause wrong client IPs, broken redirects and insecure cookies; sloppy shutdowns drop requests on every deploy.
concepts.body:
In production Express almost always sits behind a **reverse proxy** — a server that receives requests from the internet and forwards them to your app — or a load balancer (nginx, a cloud provider's load balancer, a Kubernetes ingress). It usually handles the HTTPS encryption itself (**TLS termination**) and forwards plain HTTP. From Express's point of view every request then comes from the proxy, and the real client details travel in `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host`.

Express ignores those headers until you set **`trust proxy`**, because a client can forge them. Configure it to match exactly what sits in front of your app:

- `app.set("trust proxy", 1)` — trust one hop, i.e. a single load balancer. Most common.
- A number of hops, specific IPs/subnets, or `"loopback"` / `"uniquelocal"`.
- Avoid `true` (trust everything) unless you are certain all traffic passes your proxy; otherwise clients can spoof their IP.

With it set correctly, `req.ip` is the client, `req.protocol` is `https`, `req.secure` is true, so `secure` cookies get set and rate limiters key on real IPs.

Other production essentials:

- Listen on `process.env.PORT`, on all network interfaces (`0.0.0.0`) inside containers.
- `NODE_ENV=production`, dependencies installed with `npm ci --omit=dev`.
- Run `node server.js` directly as the container command, or under systemd; not `npm start`, which may not forward signals.
- Scale with multiple instances behind the load balancer; keep sessions and caches in shared stores.
- **Graceful shutdown** — stopping without dropping requests in progress: on `SIGTERM`, fail the readiness check, call `server.close()` to stop accepting connections and let in-flight requests finish, close database pools, then exit, with a timeout as a backstop.
- Align timeouts: Node's `server.keepAliveTimeout` should exceed the load balancer's idle timeout, otherwise the load balancer may reuse a connection Node just closed and return sporadic 502s.
takeaways: Set `trust proxy` to your real topology (often `1`), never blindly `true`
Then `req.ip`, `req.protocol` and secure cookies work behind TLS termination
Run node directly, NODE_ENV=production, `npm ci --omit=dev`
Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM; keepAliveTimeout above the load balancer's idle timeout
pitfalls: Leaving `trust proxy` unset so every request appears to come from the load balancer's IP.
Setting `trust proxy` to true on a directly exposed server, letting clients spoof X-Forwarded-For.

quiz.q: Behind an HTTPS load balancer, req.protocol reports "http" and secure cookies aren't set. What's the fix?
options: Install an SSL certificate in Express
Configure app.set('trust proxy', ...) for the load balancer
Use res.redirect to https on every request
quiz.explain: Without trust proxy Express ignores X-Forwarded-Proto and sees the plain HTTP hop from the proxy.

concepts.name: Inside the router: layers and matching
concepts.summary: How Express 5's router stores layers, matches paths, walks its list of layers with next(), and skips between normal and error handlers.
concepts.why: Knowing the dispatch algorithm explains ordering bugs, next('route'), mount-path rewriting and why error handlers need four arguments.
concepts.body:
An Express app is a function `(req, res)` passed to `http.createServer`. Each request is handed to the app's **router** (from the `router` package; Express 5 exposes it as `app.router`). The router owns a **stack** — here simply an array of **Layer** objects, one per `app.use` or route registration, in registration order.

Each Layer holds a compiled path matcher (path-to-regexp v8 in Express 5) and a handler:

- `app.use(path, fn)` creates a **prefix** layer: it matches `path` and anything below it on a segment boundary.
- `app.get(path, ...fns)` creates a layer whose handler is a **Route**. The Route has its own stack of layers, one per handler, each tagged with an HTTP method. Route layers match the path **exactly** (modulo trailing slash and case, by default).

Dispatch is a loop driven by `next`:

- The router walks forward from its current index until it finds a layer whose path matches, then calls it. When that layer calls `next()`, the walk resumes from the following index.
- Every layer is either a normal handler or an **error handler**, told apart by the function's **arity** — its number of declared parameters, `fn.length`: 3 or fewer for normal, 4 for error. While an error is pending, normal layers are skipped; when no error is pending, error layers are skipped. That is the entire reason the four-parameter signature matters.
- `next("route")` skips the rest of the current Route's handlers; `next("router")` exits the current router back to its parent.
- If a handler returns a promise, the router attaches a rejection handler that calls `next(err)` — the Express 5 async behaviour.

For prefix layers, the router **strips the matched prefix** from `req.url` before calling in, saves it on `req.baseUrl`, and restores both afterwards. A mounted sub-router or sub-app therefore sees relative paths.

Route params are decoded and stored on `req.params` per layer. If the stack is exhausted, control returns to Express's **finalhandler**, which sends a 404, or a 500 if an error is still pending.
takeaways: The router walks an ordered stack of Layers; `next()` resumes the walk
`app.use` layers match prefixes and rewrite `req.url`/`req.baseUrl`
Arity 4 marks error layers; pending errors skip normal layers and vice versa
`next('route')` and `next('router')` skip ahead deliberately
pitfalls: Wrapping an error handler in a helper that hides its arity, so Express no longer sees four parameters.

quiz.q: An error is pending and the next layer in the stack is (req, res, next) => {...}. What does the router do?
options: Calls it with the error as req.error
Skips it and looks for a layer with four parameters
quiz.explain: Normal layers are skipped while an error is pending; only arity-4 layers are invoked.

quiz.q: Inside a router mounted with app.use('/shop', r), a request is for /shop/cart. What is req.url within r?
quiz.explain: The router strips the mount path from req.url (saved in req.baseUrl) for the duration of the sub-router.

concepts.name: Writing reusable middleware and libraries
concepts.summary: Design configurable middleware factories that are composable, async-safe, typed and publishable.
concepts.why: Good middleware is reused across services and teams; bad middleware leaks state, swallows errors and breaks ordering.
concepts.body:
Reusable middleware is written as a **factory function**: a function that takes options and returns the middleware `(req, res, next)`. `express.json(options)`, `cors(options)` and `helmet(options)` all work this way.

Design rules that separate solid middleware from fragile middleware:

- **Validate options at creation time** and throw early, so a misconfiguration fails at startup rather than on the first request.
- **No shared mutable state between requests**, unless it's deliberate and bounded (a cache with a size limit). Per-request data goes on `res.locals` or a single, namespaced `req` property.
- **Call `next` exactly once**, or respond — never both. Forward errors with `next(err)` instead of responding with your own error format; let the application's error handler decide.
- **Be async-safe across versions.** Express 5 catches rejections, but if you also want to support Express 4 users, wrap your async body and call `next(err)` yourself.
- **Hook the response lifecycle** with `res.on("finish")` / `res.on("close")` rather than monkey-patching `res.end` where possible; `close` without `finish` means the client went away.
- **Avoid depending on Express** when you don't need it. Middleware that only uses Node's `req`/`res` plus `next` works with Express, Connect, and Node's `http` with a tiny adapter; list Express as a peer dependency (one the installing app must provide) only if you use its helpers.

For **TypeScript** users, extend Express's `Request` type through **module augmentation** (a TypeScript declaration that adds properties to another package's types) so `req.tenant` is typed, and export your option types.

**Compose** related middleware into one unit with a Router or an array — `app.use([a, b, c])` is valid — so consumers get the correct internal order for free.

Sub-applications (`app.use("/admin", adminApp)`) are the heavier form of reuse: a whole app with its own settings, emitting a `"mount"` event and exposing `adminApp.mountpath`. Test middleware on its own with a tiny app and supertest, including error and early-exit paths.
takeaways: Middleware factories validate options up front and return `(req, res, next)`
Keep per-request data in `res.locals` or one namespaced `req` field
Forward errors with `next(err)`; let the app format them
Prefer Node-level APIs and lifecycle events over monkey-patching
pitfalls: Storing request data in a variable captured by the factory, which leaks between concurrent requests.

quiz.q: A middleware factory keeps `let currentUser` in its closure and sets it per request. What's wrong?
options: It prevents next() from being called
All concurrent requests share that variable, so users can see each other's data
Express clears closures after each request
quiz.explain: The factory runs once; its closure is shared by every request handled concurrently.

concepts.name: Migrating to Express 5: changes and edge cases
concepts.summary: What changed from Express 4 to 5: path rules, async errors, removed APIs, req.query/req.body behaviour and subtle defaults.
concepts.why: Many codebases and tutorials are still on Express 4; upgrades fail on details that aren't obvious until production.
concepts.body:
Express 5 is mostly the same API with sharp edges removed. Upgrade with `npm install express@5`, run the official **codemods** — scripts that rewrite your code automatically (`npx codemod@latest @expressjs/v5-migration-recipe`), then check these areas.

**Path syntax (path-to-regexp v8)** — the most common breakage, failing at startup:

- `/*` becomes `/*splat` (or `/{*splat}` to include the root); wildcard values are **arrays** of segments.
- Optional `/:id?` becomes `{/:id}`; `/:file.:ext?` becomes `/:file{.:ext}`.
- Inline regular expressions like `/:id(\d+)` are gone; check the value in the handler or pass a `RegExp`.
- `()[]?+!` are reserved and must be escaped.

**Async errors** are forwarded automatically, so `express-async-errors` and wrapper helpers can go.

**Removed or changed APIs:**

- `app.del` → `app.delete`; `req.param(name)` removed; `res.sendfile` → `res.sendFile`.
- `res.json(obj, status)`, `res.send(status)`, `res.redirect(url, status)` → `res.status(...)` / `res.redirect(status, url)`; `res.redirect("back")` removed.
- `req.acceptsCharset` and friends pluralised (`acceptsCharsets`).
- `app.param(fn)` and `router.param` with an array of names removed.

**Behaviour changes that pass tests but bite later:**

- `req.body` is `undefined` (not `{}`) when no parser ran.
- `req.query` is a read-only getter and the default parser is "simple": nested `a[b]=1` no longer expands.
- `express.urlencoded` defaults to `extended: false`.
- `express.static` ignores dotfiles, including `/.well-known`.
- `res.status` throws on invalid codes; `res.clearCookie` ignores `maxAge`/`expires`.
- `req.host` keeps the port; `req.params` has a null prototype.
- `app.listen` passes server errors to its callback instead of throwing.

Express 5 requires Node 18+. Upgrade middleware too — some older packages assume Express 4 internals.
takeaways: Rewrite wildcards, optional params and inline regexes for path-to-regexp v8
Async rejections reach error handlers; drop wrapper libraries
Use `res.status(...)` and `res.redirect(status, url)`; `"back"` and `req.param` are gone
Watch silent changes: `req.body` undefined, read-only `req.query`, dotfiles ignored
pitfalls: Upgrading Express without updating route strings, so the app throws at startup on `/*` or `:id?`.
Code that mutates `req.query` (e.g. for defaults) silently stops working.

quiz.q: After upgrading, GET /.well-known/assetlinks.json returns 404. Why?
options: Paths starting with a dot need regex routes
express.static now ignores dotfiles by default
quiz.explain: In Express 5 the dotfiles option defaults to "ignore"; serve .well-known explicitly with dotfiles: "allow".

quiz.q: Which Express 4 route path is still valid unchanged in Express 5?
quiz.explain: Plain named parameters are unchanged; optional ?, unnamed * and inline regexes all need rewriting.
